client: I've been really struggling since I graduated back in May — I still haven't found a job in my field, and it's been eating away at me more than I expected. Every time I see someone from my graduating class post about their new position on LinkedIn, I feel this wave of shame, like I'm already falling behind and it's only been a few months. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem is pretty concrete — I just don't have a job.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely heavy — and I notice even in the way you're speaking, there's an urgency and intensity that tells me this is really pressing on you, not just a passing worry. You're right that the job search is a concrete challenge, but the shame and the comparisons you're making to classmates — that layer is something we *can* work with, because "I'm falling behind" is a thought, not a fact, and it's worth examining what evidence actually supports it versus what your mind is adding on top of an already hard situation. Would you be open to exploring where that story of "falling behind" is coming from, even as we acknowledge the very real stress of the search itself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying about it being a thought versus a fact, but honestly it's hard to hold onto that distinction when I'm literally watching people I sat next to in class announce job offers. I guess I'm willing to talk about where the story comes from, but I'm skeptical it's going to make the shame actually go away.
therapist: Your voice carries a real tension right now — there's something almost urgent in the way you're pushing back, and I want to honor that rather than gloss over it, because your skepticism makes complete sense. You're absolutely right that the gap is real — I'm not trying to talk you out of the facts — but I want to gently separate two things: the situation itself, which is genuinely hard, and the meaning your mind is attaching to it, that this gap says something about *your* worth or trajectory, which is where the shame lives. That second part is where we have some room to work, even if it doesn't make the discomfort vanish overnight.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I think I understand the distinction you're making, but the tricky part is that the shame doesn't feel like a separate add-on — it feels baked into the situation itself, like they're the same thing. When I see those LinkedIn posts, I don't first think "I don't have a job" and then separately think "therefore I'm worthless" — it all just hits at once as this one awful feeling. I'm not sure I know how to pull those two things apart in the moment.
therapist: The way you're describing this — and even the pace and pitch in your voice right now — tells me this hits fast and hard, like a single overwhelming wave rather than a sequence of thoughts you can catch and examine. That's actually really common, and it doesn't mean the distinction isn't real; it just means the thoughts have become so automatic and fused together that they feel like one thing. Part of what we can work on is slowing that moment down *after* the fact at first — not to stop the wave, but to gradually build your ability to notice the seams between the situation and the story, which gets easier with practice even when it feels impossible right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess that makes some sense — doing it after the fact feels a little less impossible than trying to catch it in real time. But I'm a little worried that even when I slow it down later, I'm just going to keep arriving at the same conclusion, like the story is going to feel just as true on reflection as it did in the moment. What would actually make me see it differently?
therapist: There's something in your voice right now — a kind of quick, searching quality — that tells me this question feels genuinely urgent to you, like you really want to know if this process can actually deliver something different rather than just recycling the same painful conclusion. What tends to shift the story isn't just re-examining it in the abstract, but actively looking for specific evidence that *contradicts* it — so instead of asking "is this shame justified?", we'd ask something like "what does my actual history say about how I handle hard stretches, and are there things about my situation that the shame conveniently leaves out?" The story feels airtight right now partly because shame is a very selective narrator, and our job is to start introducing it to the parts of the picture it's been ignoring.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing — shame as a selective narrator — actually lands a little differently than I expected, and I can see how it might be leaving things out. But when I try to think about what my history says about handling hard stretches, I honestly can't tell if I'm going to find genuinely reassuring evidence or if I'm just going to talk myself into feeling better temporarily without anything really changing. I guess I'm willing to try, but I'm not sure what counts as real contradicting evidence versus just me being overly generous with myself.
therapist: There's something meaningful in the fact that your voice is moving quickly here, almost like your mind is racing ahead to protect you from getting your hopes up — and that caution is actually worth respecting rather than trying to argue away. The difference between genuine evidence and being "overly generous" is a great question, and the answer is that we're not looking for feel-good stories — we're looking for *specific, concrete moments* where you navigated uncertainty, disappointment, or a gap between where you were and where you wanted to be, and came through it. Those moments don't have to be dramatic to count; they just have to be real, and your job isn't to spin them positively but simply to notice that the shame has been leaving them out of the story entirely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, when I actually think about specific moments... there was a stretch in my sophomore year where I failed an important exam and genuinely thought I might not make it through the program, and I did eventually turn that around. therapist: The way you're speaking right now — soft but quick, like you're working something out carefully — feels like a real shift from earlier, and I want to name that what you just did took genuine effort, because shame doesn't give up its blind spots easily. That sophomore memory is exactly the kind of evidence we're looking for, and the fact that it didn't come automatically *is* the mechanism — so one practical thing we can build is a small, specific collection of moments like that one, almost like a written list, so that when the LinkedIn wave hits and everything else disappears, you're not relying on your memory to fight back against shame in real time. You'd be reaching for something concrete you already prepared, rather than trying to think clearly in the middle of the flood.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: A written list actually makes more sense to me than some of the other things I've tried, because you're right that I can't think straight when I'm in the middle of it. therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, pitched high, like you're thinking through this in real time — tells me you're genuinely engaging with this rather than just going through the motions, and that matters. The worry that shame will feel more "honest" than the list is actually one of the most important things you've said, because it names something real: shame often *masquerades* as clarity, like it's the one telling you the truth while everything else is just wishful thinking. Part of what we can work on is recognizing that feeling as a signal that shame is doing its selective narrator thing again — not a reason to put the list down, but actually a cue to pick it up.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That reframe — that the "shame feels more honest" sensation is actually a cue to pick up the list rather than put it down — is something I want to hold onto, because it gives me something to do with that feeling instead of just being steamrolled by it. The fact that you're already thinking about the friction points is exactly the right instinct, and we can spend some time figuring out the specific format that would feel least easy to dismiss when shame is telling you not to bother.
